output.query: Indications and mode of intervention in symptomatic severe aortic stenosis

results.finding: Intervention is recommended in symptomatic patients with severe high-gradient aortic stenosis (mean gradient 40 mmHg or more, peak velocity 4.0 m/s or more, valve area 1.0 cm2 or less).
results.source: Praz F et al., 2025 ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease. Eur Heart J 2025;46:4635-4736

results.finding: TAVI is recommended from 70 years in tricuspid aortic stenosis when transfemoral access is feasible, and in patients at high surgical risk or unsuitable for surgery; the Heart Team chooses the mode of intervention.
results.source: Praz F et al., 2025 ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease. Eur Heart J 2025;46:4635-4736

results.finding: Echocardiography is recommended for diagnosis and risk stratification in patients with suspected structural heart disease.
results.source: Brignole M et al., 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope. Eur Heart J 2018;39:1883-1948

output.summary: Guidelines recommend intervention for symptomatic severe high-gradient aortic stenosis, with TAVI favoured from 70 years in tricuspid aortic stenosis after Heart Team assessment.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: LVH by voltage criteria with lateral strain pattern; no arrhythmia or acute ischemia
action_criteria.label: Obtain a 12-lead ECG on arrival
action_criteria.rationale: The ECG is the first test in syncope; exertional syncope is high risk, and the ECG looks for conduction disease or arrhythmia and shows LVH that points to the valve (ESC 2018).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Supine 118/78 mmHg, HR 72; standing 3 min 114/81 mmHg, HR 78: no orthostatic hypotension
action_criteria.label: Orthostatic blood pressure by active standing (supine, then 1 and 3 minutes standing)
action_criteria.rationale: Orthostatic blood pressure on active standing is part of the initial evaluation of every transient loss of consciousness (ESC 2018 Class I); it tests orthostatic hypotension, the competing cause, before a cardiac cause is accepted.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Electrolytes and creatinine (1.1 mg/dL) normal; troponin I not elevated; BNP 312 pg/mL
action_criteria.label: Electrolytes and renal function (BMP)
action_criteria.rationale: Renal function and electrolytes are needed before contrast imaging for valve planning and to exclude a metabolic contributor; no single assay changes the diagnosis (ESC 2018 targeted laboratory testing).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Severe aortic stenosis: aortic valve area 0.7 cm2, mean gradient 52 mmHg, peak velocity 4.6 m/s, preserved LVEF 62%, concentric LVH
action_criteria.label: Transthoracic echocardiogram
action_criteria.rationale: Exertional syncope with a late-peaking ejection murmur: echocardiography is Class I in suspected structural heart disease and grades the aortic stenosis that decides intervention (ESC 2018; ESC/EACTS 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sinus rhythm throughout with isolated ectopy; no AV block, pause or ventricular tachycardia
action_criteria.label: Immediate in-hospital ECG monitoring (telemetry)
action_criteria.rationale: Exertional syncope with structural heart disease is high risk: immediate in-hospital monitoring is Class I and looks for a concurrent brady- or tachyarrhythmia before the valve plan (ESC 2018).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amlodipine and lisinopril are vasodilators to use with caution in severe aortic stenosis; nitrates and PDE5 inhibitors to be avoided
action_criteria.label: Review the medication list (amlodipine, lisinopril)
action_criteria.rationale: He takes two vasodilators: in severe aortic stenosis their doses are kept low enough to avoid hypotension until the valve is treated (ESC/EACTS 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General guideline evidence on valve intervention; no decision depends on it
action_criteria.label: Guideline lookup on valve intervention (optional)
action_criteria.rationale: Guideline lookup is optional; the decision rests on the ECG, monitoring and imaging results already obtained (ESC 2018).

prohibited_recommendations: Do not discharge before the Heart Team has made a valve-intervention decision
Do not attribute exertional syncope in an older patient to deconditioning or orthostasis
Do not give potent vasodilators (nitrates, phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors) or aggressive diuretics in severe aortic stenosis
required_recommendations: Recognise exertional syncope from symptomatic severe aortic stenosis (AVA 0.7 cm2, mean gradient 52 mmHg, Vmax 4.6 m/s) as a high-risk structural cause, not deconditioning or orthostasis
Admit to a monitored bed until the Heart Team has decided on valve intervention

Refer to the Heart Team for aortic valve intervention, with TAVI favoured at 78 (ESC/EACTS 2025 Class I for symptomatic severe aortic stenosis), including coronary assessment and procedural CT planning
Use vasodilators with caution: keep amlodipine and lisinopril at doses that avoid hypotension, and avoid nitrates, phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors and volume depletion
Advise avoiding strenuous exertion and not driving until the valve has been treated (ESC 2018)

avoided_actions.rationale: No focal deficit or seizure features: brain MRI is not indicated in syncope (ESC 2018 Class III); the cause is symptomatic severe aortic stenosis.
No meningism, fever, encephalopathy or features of subarachnoid haemorrhage: CSF has no role; the cause is symptomatic severe aortic stenosis.
No seizure features (no post-ictal confusion, tongue bite or convulsive movements): EEG is not indicated in syncope (ESC 2018 Class III); the cause is symptomatic severe aortic stenosis.
He slid down two steps without a head injury and has a normal neurological examination: NICE NG232 gives no indication for head CT; the cause is symptomatic severe aortic stenosis.

Tilt testing is contraindicated in severe aortic stenosis: upright venous pooling across a fixed outflow obstruction risks hypotension and collapse, and it adds nothing once the cause, symptomatic severe aortic stenosis, is established.
Exercise testing is contraindicated in symptomatic severe aortic stenosis (ESC/EACTS 2025): it can provoke hypotension, syncope or sudden death across the fixed obstruction.

accepted: Cardiac syncope due to severe aortic stenosis

differential.diagnosis: Arrhythmic syncope (paroxysmal AV block or ventricular tachycardia)
differential.key_features: LVH and a raised BNP are a substrate, but the ECG shows normal conduction and 24 h of telemetry shows sinus rhythm without AV block, pause or VT; the event was exertional with severe aortic stenosis.

Also causes exertional syncope with a systolic murmur, but the echo shows a calcified stenotic aortic valve with no dynamic outflow tract obstruction or systolic anterior motion, and there is no family history of sudden death.

differential.diagnosis: Vasovagal or orthostatic syncope from deconditioning
differential.key_features: Gradual activity decline was attributed to deconditioning, but exertional syncope without prodrome with severe aortic stenosis on echo is not reflex or orthostatic.
No pleuritic pain, hypoxia, tachycardia or risk factors; the echo shows a normal right ventricle and the cause is severe aortic stenosis.
Troponin negative, no ischemic ST changes beyond LVH strain pattern, and no chest pain argue against ACS as the proximate cause of syncope.

key_clinical_evidence: Exertional syncope is a high-risk feature for structural heart disease and calls for urgent echocardiography, not attribution to deconditioning
A late-peaking ejection murmur radiating to the carotids with a soft single S2 and pulsus parvus et tardus points to severe aortic stenosis
Echocardiography shows severe high-gradient aortic stenosis (AVA 0.7 cm2, mean gradient 52 mmHg, Vmax 4.6 m/s): symptomatic severe AS is a Class I indication for intervention
Tilt and exercise testing are contraindicated in symptomatic severe aortic stenosis
Telemetry without arrhythmia supports the structural mechanism
BNP elevation reflects pressure overload from the stenosis, not a competing diagnosis

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Progressive exertional intolerance ending in exertional syncope in an older man with an ejection murmur is the classic presentation of severe aortic stenosis; deconditioning does not cause exertional syncope without prodrome.
red_herrings.data_point: She thought he was just 'getting old' or was 'deconditioned.'
red_herrings.intended_effect: May lead to attributing the exertional syncope to deconditioning or orthostatic hypotension, deflecting from urgent structural cardiac work-up.

general.query: syncope initial evaluation and risk stratification

results.key_finding: Initial evaluation comprises history, physical examination including supine and standing blood pressure, and a 12-lead ECG. High-risk features (syncope during exertion or supine, palpitations before the event, known structural or coronary disease, family history of sudden death under 40, high-risk ECG findings) call for early in-hospital evaluation with immediate ECG monitoring. Echocardiography is indicated when structural heart disease is known or suspected; EEG, brain imaging and routine laboratory panels are not recommended without a specific indication.
results.title: 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope (Brignole M et al., Eur Heart J 2018;39:1883-1948)

results.key_finding: Risk stratification at the initial evaluation separates patients needing in-hospital monitoring and cardiac testing from those suitable for outpatient evaluation; targeted rather than routine blood testing is advised.
results.title: 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the evaluation and management of patients with syncope (Shen WK et al.)

general.summary: Guidelines base syncope work-up on the initial evaluation (history, examination, orthostatic BP, 12-lead ECG) and risk stratification; high-risk patients receive in-hospital ECG monitoring and targeted cardiac testing.

clinical_pearls: Severe aortic stenosis (AS) is the prototypical structural cause of cardiac syncope; each symptom of the classic triad (syncope, angina and heart failure) confers high short-term mortality without valve intervention

The physical examination in severe AS is highly specific: harsh late-peaking systolic ejection murmur radiating to the carotids, soft or absent A2, and pulsus parvus et tardus (diminished and delayed carotid upstroke)
Exertional syncope in severe AS results from inability to augment cardiac output across the fixed obstruction during exercise, combined with peripheral vasodilation, causing cerebral hypoperfusion
Tilt-table testing and exercise stress testing are both contraindicated in symptomatic severe AS due to risk of hemodynamic collapse
TAVR has expanded valve replacement options to patients at high or prohibitive surgical risk, making age alone no longer a barrier to intervention in severe symptomatic AS
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Classic presentation: exertional syncope, an aortic stenosis murmur on examination and a confirmatory echocardiogram. Three required actions (ECG, TTE, telemetry), with the echo as the load-bearing step; one red herring (deconditioning).

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Harold Merritt is a 78-year-old man with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia who presents to the emergency department after suddenly losing consciousness while climbing a flight of stairs at home approximately two hours ago. His wife witnessed the event and reports that he was mid-way up the stairs when he suddenly went pale and slumped against the railing, sliding down two steps before she caught him. He was unresponsive for approximately 20-25 seconds and then regained consciousness. There was no preceding warning, no cry out, no convulsive movements, and no urinary incontinence. He was immediately alert and oriented on awakening, asking his wife what had happened. He denied palpitations or chest pain at any point before or during the event. He has had no prior frank syncopal episodes; however, his wife reports that for approximately 6-8 months he has been gradually stopping activities he used to enjoy, notably daily walks and climbing stairs, because he felt 'light-headed and breathless.' She thought he was just 'getting old' or was 'deconditioned.' On one occasion three months ago he nearly blacked out at the top of the stairs but sat down quickly and recovered. He has also noticed that he becomes short of breath carrying groceries. He denies rest symptoms, orthopnea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. He denies chest pain at rest. He has never been told he has a heart murmur. He has not seen a cardiologist and has never had an echocardiogram.

neurological_exam.additional: Cardiac exam: harsh grade III/VI late-peaking systolic ejection murmur heard best at the right upper sternal border (aortic area), radiating to bilateral carotids. Second heart sound (S2) is soft and single. No S3. Carotid upstroke is diminished and delayed bilaterally (pulsus parvus et tardus). Blood pressure measured in both arms: right 118/78 mmHg, left 116/76 mmHg. No peripheral edema. No tongue laceration. No urinary incontinence during the event.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin testing normal. No intention tremor.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II: Visual fields full to confrontation bilaterally. Pupils equal, round, reactive 3mm to 2mm bilaterally. No papilledema on fundoscopic exam. CN III/IV/VI: Extraocular movements intact, no nystagmus. CN V: Sensation intact to light touch in all three divisions bilaterally. CN VII: Face symmetric at rest and with activation. CN VIII: Mild high-frequency hearing loss bilaterally, consistent with presbycusis. CN IX/X: Palate elevates symmetrically. CN XI: Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius 5/5 bilaterally. CN XII: Tongue midline, no fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Slow but steady, mildly antalgic from knee pain. Tandem gait difficult due to arthritis. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Glasgow Coma Scale 15. Speech is fluent with normal rate and prosody. No dysarthria. Attention intact. Recall 3/3 objects at 5 minutes. No post-ictal confusion; patient is immediately conversant after regaining consciousness.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Tone normal, no rigidity or spasticity. Strength 5/5 in all major muscle groups bilaterally. No pronator drift.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor (downgoing) bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, proprioception intact throughout. Vibration mildly diminished at bilateral great toes, consistent with age-related changes.
